title: The Greatest Rotation That Never Was
subtitle: 25 years ago, Florida assembled a group of Young Guns who became All-Stars, champions and longtime MLB starters. They just barely got the chance to actually pitch together.
contentHtml:
These days, Ryan Dempster is known as the affable co-host of MLB Network’s Intentional Talk, after closing the books on a 16-year major-league career that saw him win 132 games, become a fan-favorite with the Chicago Cubs and win a championship with the Boston Red Sox.

But before any of that, he was the elder statesman on a Florida Marlins rotation that had as much talent as any in baseball in its day. (“The Marlins have baseball’s top young staff,” wrote no less an expert than Tony Gwynn in an ESPN op-ed.) It was a future-focused rotation with four of five members peaking in the Top 20 of Baseball America’s prospect rankings, and all five being able to touch 96+ MPH with their fastballs at a time when the MLB starter average was around 88 MPH.

And how old was Dempster when he earned that grizzled-veteran status? Just 23, when he was Florida’s opening-day starter in 2001 — that’s how precocious this pitching staff was.

Subscribe now

Twenty-five years ago, the Marlins’ “Young Guns” quintet of Dempster, Brad Penny, A.J. Burnett, Matt Clement and Josh Beckett were going to be big. And they did eventually do some big things in the big leagues. But the biggest thing about them was how quickly they were broken apart, before anyone got to see what they could do all together. They were the greatest rotation that basically never actually got to exist.

In their MLB careers overall, Burnett (164), Beckett (138), Dempster (132), Penny (121) and Clement (87) combined to win 642 games. They collectively made nine All-Star Games and won five World Series rings — with Beckett being named MVP of the 2003 Fall Classic. Their combined 135.9 career Wins Above Replacement (WAR) ranked seventh among the best five-starter groups found on any team in 2001.1 The Young Guns ended up being a very good (and occasionally great) set of starting pitchers, albeit something less than you might have expected from those ‘90s Braves comparisons getting thrown around at the time.

What sets them apart, though, is how little of that damage was done with Florida — and especially collectively as Marlins. Their time in Miami only overlapped for one single season, 2001, and even then Beckett did not make his MLB debut until September 4 of the season. The Young Guns made exactly TWO trips, Nos. 1-5, through the rotation order in their entire history: September 9-21, and then September 26-30, 2001:

After Burnett won the season finale in Atlanta to end 2001, the offseason got underway as Florida looked ahead to the first complete season with its full five-man starting corps.

Except, that never actually happened.

Days before the ‘02 season was set to begin, Clement was traded to the Cubs along with Antonio Alfonseca for Dontrelle Willis — the “D-Train” — and Julián Tavárez (among others). Willis was much younger and ended up having more career WAR than Clement, so it’s hard to argue it wasn’t the right move, aside from bringing a symbolic end to Florida’s vaunted young rotation. Later that summer, as Florida was hovering around .500, Marlins brass also dealt away Dempster to the Reds for Juan Encarnación and a few other players. The Young Guns were no more.

Despite breaking up a seemingly generational rotation and struggling down the stretch in 2002, the Marlins did lay some of the groundwork for their eventual win in the ‘03 World Series. Beckett, Burnett and Penny would stay with the club not only through that run but also the next few years, before being scattered to more expensive teams. With a championship to show for it, you can’t really say Florida’s teardown was some great organizational failure.

But the gutting of the Young Guns still left behind a surprising “what if” in baseball history — as few collections of starters went on to rack up more WAR for other teams down the line (relative to how little they did together for their original team) than Florida’s set of young aces.

Simply summing up the net value produced by a team’s Top 5 future starters (according to rest-of-career WAR) through that season, minus all future WAR for other franchises, we arrive at Florida ranked with the seventh-most negative differential since the dawn of the modern five-man rotation in the 1970s:

The ones that got away

The others ranked above Florida either featured notorious cases of teams shipping away future Hall of Fame aces — the Mets’ trade of Nolan Ryan, the Expos’ trade of Randy Johnson — or were teams featuring Greg Maddux (who needs no introduction) and/or Jamie Moyer, the ageless crafty-lefty who produced three times as many WAR from age 34 (!) onward as he had beforehand.

One fascinating thing about the Marlins’ version, however, is they didn’t rely on a singular ace — no Ryan, no Johnson, no Maddux — to carry them up this list. The best of the Young Guns by career WAR was Beckett with 36.1, followed closely by Burnett at 35.8, but those are comparatively modest totals that left each well short of Hall of Fame consideration. What makes Florida’s hard-throwing quintet special is that all produced at least some level of success, with Dempster compiling 25.5 WAR, Penny 22.7 (which feels low, tbh) and Clement 15.7.

Very rarely do you hit on ALL five pitching prospects in a given crop, in terms of each becoming a good MLB pitcher for a long time. To wit: Aside from Clement at nine big-league seasons, each of Beckett (14), Penny (14), Dempster (16) and Burnett (17!) spent at least 14 years in the majors.

To capture this top-to-bottom effect, we can calculate a weighted version of our ranking from above — again taking the Top 5 future starters on a team, but adjusting their to-date and rest-of-career-with-other-teams WAR according to a scheme that assigns 100 percent weight to the fifth-ranked pitcher, 80 percent to No. 4, and so forth down to 20 percent for No. 1. This will have the effect of rewarding deep potential rotations who nonetheless did most of their damage for squads other than the one they were collected on.

When we account for their depth, Beckett, Burnett, Dempster, Penny and Clement indeed emerge as the most potential-laden modern rotation that never really got the chance to pitch together.

Aside from 10 game-days in September 2001, the Marlins’ fireballing young rotation never actually existed outside the minds of fans, or maybe those of us who played MLB video games in the era (where the young pitching made Florida a far more desirable team to play as than in reality).

Clement even predicted that outcome in Spring Training of 2002. “The way baseball is,” he said at the time, “five or six years from now, if two of us are still together, I’d be surprised, unfortunately.”

Sometimes the hype around a crop of pitching prospects is simply wrong — see the Mets’ infamous Generation K for an example of that. The irony of the Young Guns, though, is that the hype was mostly right: All five became All-Stars, four won World Series rings, and each lasted a long time in the majors. Florida really did assemble a special rotation 25 years ago. It just never became Florida’s rotation in any meaningful sense.

In other words, the Greatest Rotation That Never Was really was great. It was just great almost entirely somewhere else.
